title: Emrys and the Room
premise: Folklorist Lena Eriksen arrives in the isolated village of Hollowmere to record its songs, only to find every tune ends mid-verse, as if cut off by a bell that was melted down in 1911. When the phantom bell rings, Lena is pulled into 'the Room'—a shifting space beneath the village where the drowned of the old well wait to be counted, and where belonging is measured by how many times you let them sing your name. As the well refills toward the final count, Lena must choose between the identity she clings to and the found family forming among the villagers who refuse to sing twice. In the end, Lena sings the forbidden verse herself, breaking the count, emptying the Room, and staying in Hollowmere not as an outsider recording it but as one of its own.
about_author: Orsen Delacroix is the pen name of a former archivist of parish records who spent a decade cataloguing churches that no longer exist. He writes horror about places that remember more than the people living in them.

chapters.title: The Song That Stops
chapters.summary: Lena Eriksen arrives in Hollowmere with recording equipment and professional skepticism, interviewing elderly residents about folk songs. Every singer stops at the same verse, pale and refusing to continue. POV: Lena. Emotional beat: curiosity curdling into unease as he realizes the silence is coordinated, not accidental.

chapters.title: A Village That Won't Look Up
chapters.summary: Lena explores Hollowmere's church, finding the bell tower empty except for a rope worn smooth by use. The vicar, Maren Oduya, warns him gently that some questions are counted as answers. POV: Lena. Emotional beat: isolation deepening; the village's warmth feels like a wall built around him.

chapters.title: Nineteen Eleven
chapters.summary: In the parish archive, Lena finds records of the bell's melting and a list of names marked 'counted.' A photograph shows villagers standing around the well, mouths open mid-song. POV: Lena. Emotional beat: the thrill of discovery shadowed by the sense that the archive is watching him back.

chapters.title: The Bell Rings
chapters.summary: At dusk, a bell tolls from the empty tower. The whole village freezes, then bows their heads. Lena alone looks up—and the sound reaches into his chest like a hand. POV: Lena. Emotional beat: terror and awe; his unbelief cracks for the first time.

chapters.title: Down the Well Rope
chapters.summary: Drawn against his will, Lena descends the dry well and enters the Room: a vast dark space where voices hum the unfinished verse. Figures without faces turn toward him, patient. POV: Lena. Emotional beat: claustrophobic dread mixed with a horrifying flicker of comfort—he has never felt expected anywhere before.

chapters.title: The Count Begins
chapters.summary: The Room's presence, called the Tallyman, explains nothing but shows Lena a rising number scratched into stone. Each villager who dies or leaves adds to it. POV: Lena. Emotional beat: cold comprehension; this is arithmetic, not haunting, and arithmetic can be beaten.

chapters.title: Maren's Confession
chapters.summary: Vicar Maren admits her family has kept the count for generations, singing half-songs to slow it. She lost her brother to the well as a child. POV: Maren. Emotional beat: guilt and tenderness entwined; she sees in Lena both a danger and a hope.

chapters.title: Songs for the Drowned
chapters.summary: Maren teaches Lena the protective half-verses and introduces him to the Oduya household—her niece Ida, her taciturn brother Tomas. For the first time, someone sets a place for Lena at a table. POV: Lena. Emotional beat: reluctant warmth; found family beginning to form around shared fear.

chapters.title: Ida Hears It Too
chapters.summary: Twelve-year-old Ida confesses she hears the bell even when others don't, and the Room calls her by name. Lena realizes the Tallyman wants a successor. POV: Ida. Emotional beat: a child's loneliness mirroring Lena's own; his protectiveness ignites.

chapters.title: The Rule of Twice
chapters.summary: Researching the folklore, Lena deciphers why songs are never sung twice: repetition completes the verse, and a completed verse completes a name. The village survives by leaving everything unfinished. POV: Lena. Emotional beat: intellectual triumph turning to horror—the rule also means nothing here is ever allowed to be whole.

chapters.title: Tomas Breaks
chapters.summary: Grief-stricken Tomas sings a full song over his dead wife's grave. That night the water level in the well rises visibly, and the count jumps. POV: Tomas. Emotional beat: devastating love weaponized against him; the cost of wholeness made flesh.

chapters.title: What the Water Remembers
chapters.summary: Lena dreams himself into the Room voluntarily, seeking the drowned. They show him 1911: the villagers melted the bell to stop a previous count, drowning the ringer instead. POV: Lena. Emotional beat: moral vertigo—Hollowmere's survival was founded on a sacrifice everyone pretends was weather.

chapters.title: The Outsider Question
chapters.summary: Some villagers blame Lena for accelerating the count; eggs crack against the church door. Maren defends him publicly, binding her family to his fate. POV: Maren. Emotional beat: solidarity forged under pressure; Lena is no longer a guest but kin, with all the danger that implies.

chapters.title: Ida's Invitation
chapters.summary: The Room offers Ida a bargain: come now, spare the village. She nearly walks to the well at midnight before Lena and Maren pull her back. POV: Ida. Emotional beat: heartbreak and resolve; the family closes ranks around its youngest.

chapters.title: Halfway Down
chapters.summary: Lena descends again to negotiate, offering himself in Ida's place. The Tallyman considers him—a man with no family, no roots, no one to sing his name—and finds the offer almost acceptable. POV: Lena. Emotional beat: self-erasure confronted; he realizes he's been volunteering all his life.

chapters.title: The Verse No One Wrote Down
chapters.summary: Among the drowned, Lena learns there is a final verse that empties the Room—but it must be sung by someone who chooses to belong, sung twice, willingly. No villager has ever dared. POV: Lena. Emotional beat: dawning purpose; the thing he never had is the key.

chapters.title: The Well Refills
chapters.summary: Rain floods the valley; the well rises past every mark. The village evacuates its children while adults stand vigil with lanterns. POV: Tomas. Emotional beat: communal fear transmuted into stubborn love; Tomas, broken, becomes the family's spine.

chapters.title: Countdown at the Churchyard
chapters.summary: The bell tolls continuously now. The count nears completion as the last families gather, and the Tallyman's voice begins reading names aloud—including Maren's. POV: Maren. Emotional beat: terror at the threshold of surrender, held together by the people beside her.

chapters.title: Emrys
chapters.summary: In the Room, the drowned reveal they have been calling Lena by an older name—Emrys—the name he'd have been given by the family that abandoned him. Belonging, they say, was always on offer. POV: Lena/Emrys. Emotional beat: identity shattered and remade; he accepts the name and claims it as his own choice.

chapters.title: Sung Twice
chapters.summary: Climax: Emrys stands at the well's edge with the Oduyas holding the rope, and sings the final verse—twice, complete, unafraid. The bell shatters mid-toll, the water drains to dust, and the Tallyman's count unravels into silence. POV: Emrys. Emotional beat: triumphant grief; wholeness achieved at the price of the world he used to believe in.

chapters.title: After the Counting
chapters.summary: Hollowmere wakes changed: songs can finally be finished, graves stay closed, the tower stands quiet. The village buries the drowned properly and, for the first time in a century, sings at a wedding. POV: Maren. Emotional beat: tender release; mourning completed rather than deferred.

chapters.title: The Name at the Table
chapters.summary: Epilogue: Emrys stays in Hollowmere, teaching Ida the full songs, his recorder finally capturing endings. At Sunday dinner, Maren sets his place without asking. POV: Emrys. Emotional beat: quiet belonging earned; the folklorist who came to record a village has become one of its verses.
